hints: Think about whether light delivers its energy smoothly and continuously like a wave, or in tiny separate bursts.
Remember what type of energy a photon carries - it is the basic unit of all electromagnetic radiation, from radio to gamma, with energy $E = hf$.
walkthrough:
**Move Away From the Continuous Wave Idea**
Think of light not as a steady flow but as arriving in tiny, indivisible lumps. Each lump cannot be split - an electron either absorbs a whole photon or nothing at all. That is what we mean by discrete or quantised.

**Link It to Electromagnetic Radiation**
All EM waves, including visible light, X-rays and so on, are made up of these packets. So a complete definition needs both ideas: a photon is a packet or quantum of energy, and that energy belongs to electromagnetic radiation. Its energy is given by $$E = hf$$ where $h$ is the Planck constant and $f$ is the frequency.
Final answer: A photon is a discrete packet (quantum) of energy of electromagnetic radiation.

hints: Think about what wave theory predicts for brighter light - more energy - and compare it with what actually happens to the speed of emitted electrons when you turn up the intensity.
walkthrough:
**What Intensity Means for Photons**
Increasing intensity at constant frequency means more photons per second arriving, but each individual photon still has the same energy $E = hf$. So more electrons can be released per second, but each one gets no more energy.

**Why This Proves Particles**
If light were purely a wave, brighter light would give more energy to each electron and make faster electrons. In the photoelectric effect this does not happen - the maximum $E_k$ of electrons stays the same when intensity increases. That only makes sense if energy arrives in separate photon packets.
Final answer: Increasing the intensity of light does not increase the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons.

hints: Start with darkness - look at Fig. 11.1 and decide which band holds the electrons and which band is empty when no light energy is supplied.
Recall what is needed for conduction - free mobile charge carriers in the conduction band - and why a full valence band alone gives very high resistance.
Think about what a photon of light can give to an electron in the valence band to help it cross the forbidden band.
When an electron leaves the valence band, consider what is left behind and why that vacancy also acts as a mobile charge carrier.
Link the total number of free carriers in light versus dark to the change in resistance.
walkthrough:
**In Darkness - No Free Carriers**
In a semiconductor the valence band is full of electrons but those electrons are bound and cannot move freely to carry current. The conduction band, where electrons are free to move throughout the solid, is essentially empty in darkness. With almost no mobile charge carriers, the material cannot conduct well, so resistance is very high.

**In Light - Photons Supply the Jump Energy**
Light arrives as photons each of energy $$E = hf$$ When a photon is absorbed by an electron in the valence band, that electron gains the whole photon energy. If this is large enough to bridge the forbidden band (the band gap), the electron is promoted up into the conduction band.

**Two Types of Carrier Are Created**
The promoted electron is now free in the conduction band and can move as a charge carrier. Just as important, it leaves behind a vacancy called a hole in the valence band. Neighbouring electrons can move into that hole, so the hole itself moves and acts as a positive mobile charge carrier.

**More Carriers Means Lower Resistance**
Resistance depends on how many charge carriers are available. In daylight there are many more conduction electrons plus valence holes than in darkness. With a much larger number density of mobile carriers, the same p.d. drives a larger current, so $$R = V/I$$ decreases. This is photoconduction, the principle of an LDR.

Final answer: In darkness the conduction band is essentially empty with electrons only in the valence band, so there are very few free charge carriers and resistance is very high. Incident light photons give valence electrons energy to jump the forbidden band into the conduction band, leaving holes in the valence band. Both the conduction electrons and holes are mobile charge carriers, so the increased carrier number in light greatly decreases resistance.
